seoDescription: Learn how to add posts to your WordPress site from the frontend using the WP REST API and vanilla JavaScript. This tutorial covers setting up a bare-bones theme, fetching existing posts, and authenticating with the JWT Authentication for WP API plugin. You'll see how to correctly configure the JWT secret key, generate and store an authentication token in local storage, and then use that token to programmatically create new posts and custom post types with a fetch request, complete with an authorization bearer token header.

chapters.title: Introduction: Adding Posts from the Frontend
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the video's goal: using the WP REST API to add posts to a WordPress database from the frontend.

chapters.title: Project Setup and Environment
chapters.description: This chapter explains the bare-bones theme and vanilla JavaScript setup used for the demonstration.

chapters.title: Fetching Existing Posts with REST API
chapters.description: Learn how to use vanilla JavaScript's fetch API to retrieve and log all existing posts from the WordPress REST API endpoint.

chapters.title: Introducing JWT for Authentication
chapters.description: This section introduces the necessity of authentication and presents the "JWT Authentication for WP API" plugin as the solution.

chapters.title: Configuring the JWT Plugin
chapters.description: Follow the steps to request an authentication token, troubleshoot the "forbidden" error, and correctly set the `JWT_AUTH_SECRET_KEY` in `wp-config.php`.

chapters.title: Storing the Authentication Token
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to save the received JWT token into the browser's local storage for future API requests.

chapters.title: Building the Frontend Interface
chapters.description: Create a simple HTML button and the corresponding JavaScript function structure to trigger the post creation process.

chapters.title: Creating Posts Programmatically
chapters.description: This chapter details how to construct and send a POST request with an Authorization header to create a new WordPress post.

chapters.title: Working with Custom Post Types
chapters.description: Learn how to adapt the code to add entries to custom post types, such as products, by changing the REST API endpoint.

chapters.title: Conclusion
chapters.description: The video concludes with a summary of the concepts covered and points to the GitHub repository for the source code.

transcription:
## Introduction: Adding Posts from the Frontend

In this episode, I'm going to quickly show you how you can add posts to your WordPress installation or how you can save posts to your database but from the frontend. And of course, using WP REST API.

## Project Setup and Environment

Before we begin, let's just discuss setup a little bit. So, I'm using a theme which is called watch learn and as you will see, this theme is very very bare-bones. So, it only has this index.php file and style.css.

You need to have style.css so that you can define your theme and I have this index.php file which just says hello world to us and that's about it. If we take a look at it, this is our theme, right? If I refresh it, you just get hello world. You of course need to activate that theme.

I'm using a theme because I want to do this with vanilla JavaScript but of course, in the real world, you would probably not even be using a theme. You would probably be using something like Next or some other JS framework to get your data. But of course, you can use this inside of a theme also if you need it. So, this is going to help us get going very quickly and I'm going to show you how you can add posts or add custom post types to your WordPress database.

## Fetching Existing Posts with REST API

As I said, I'm just going to be using vanilla JavaScript for this and I'm going to open some script tags right here and first of all, let me just show you how you can firstly get the posts in your theme so that you can display them.

And this is very easy and actually we covered a lot of similar things to this in the Next.js and Strapi series and practically using the same code because of course Next.js is just React plus vanilla JavaScript, right? So, you would just do something like this. My domain name is wprest.test.

I'm using Laravel Valet to set up my site. So, that's why I'm getting this domain but you can of course use something like MAMP, XAMPP, WAMP, whatever you like to use. So, we are just fetching the posts.

Then we are returning that response and then we are just console logging out that response. If I save this, go to the browser, refresh it, as you can see, we are getting the posts from our REST API's posts route and you can see all of the posts right here. Of course, if you were using something like Next.js or Nuxt, this would be pretty easy to display on your site but if you are using vanilla JavaScript, it will be a little bit harder because you would have to interact with the DOM and then displaying that and then displaying all of it in the DOM and so on.

But we are not going to be doing none of that in this episode. I'm just going to show you how you can get the posts, how you can authenticate and then how you can add the posts into your database so that you get the general idea of how this works and then of course, you can expand on that to suit your needs, right? Okay. So, this is the way we would we would get the posts.

## Introducing JWT for Authentication

Now, how do we add the posts?

Well, first of all, we need to authenticate because you can't just add the posts to your WordPress site without entering username or password, right?

So, to do that, we are going to install—I already actually installed it—you would install this plugin right here. And this plugin is called JWT authentication for WP API. So, we are going to be using this plugin and this plugin is just going to add a REST API route to our system that we can connect to, get the token and then we can use that token to add data to our site as you will see in just a few seconds. So, of course, install this first.

## Configuring the JWT Plugin

Take a look at the documentation because this is very important. As you will see, it this will not work out of the box just yet.

So, let's just try it out. So, to authenticate, what you need to do, you need to go to your code editor and do something like this. Okay. So, we are now fetching another route which is called `wp-json-jwt-auth-v1-token`.

So, this is the route that we are getting from our plugin. And then we want to send that request with a POST method. Of course, you send some headers and in this body, you would send username and password. For me, that's admin and test123, right? So, you would send all of that and then you would wait for the response and you can actually console log out that response.

I'm going to remove this for now because we just want to test this out first. So, if I save this and go to my browser and now if we refresh the page, as you can see, we get this forbidden right here and this is because we need to set up JWT auth secret key in our in our WP config before we can continue. And you can read about that right here in the documentation. So, this won't work without this. So, you can just go to your WP config and as you can see, I already had it set it up. It's just commented out. So, I would define my JWT auth secret key and add a key to it. Now, to get the key, it says in the documentation that you can just go right here.

paste it in. And now you would get some random keys. So, you can take any one of these and set it to your JWT auth secret key. Okay. So, you got that set up, save it and now let's try to test out our site.

Refresh it and now as you can see, we are actually getting that token.

## Storing the Authentication Token

So, this is our token right here. Of course, to use it, we would need to save the token and we are going to do that with local storage. So, I'm just going to save that token into our local storage like this.

So, at the end of this function, so we are getting the response. We are console logging out user.token. So, this is our token and now I want to save that token to my local storage. And I just do this. Local storage set item JWT and we are sending the user token. So, if I save this, go to my browser, refresh it again and now if we go to application, as you can see, in our local storage for our site, we have JWT token set up.

Of course, probably in the production version of this, when you are doing this for a live site, you would probably want to save this inside of a cookie instead of a local storage. But for now, we are just going to save it here so that we can access it whenever we need it. And of course, we are going to need to access it when we want to add some posts to our site because to add something to your site, you need to authenticate yourself and we are going to be doing that right now.

## Building the Frontend Interface

So, first of all, I don't want to add the post on the page load. So, I'm just going to create a button which is going to when we click it, add a post to our website. Okay. And my button is going to have a class of JS add post. It's going to say add post and that's about it.

Next, I'm going to create a function which I'm going to just call add post so that I can access it when I add event listener to my button. I'm just going to say to that button, okay, whenever someone clicks it, just run this function. And what this function is going to do, it's just going to add a post to our site using fetch of course.

## Creating Posts Programmatically

Okay. So, first of all, I just add fetch. Then we add method here. After that, we want to add some headers and now the important thing is we need to send authorization header. So, to send authorization header, you need to send it with a bearer and to do that and actually we did that in the Next.js Strapi episodes, you would just say bearer and then send your JWT token. So, we set up bearer and we get the JWT token from local storage. So, you just do local storage.getItem JWT. That's about it.

Next thing you need to send is you need to send the body. So, of course, you need to populate your post. Of course, we are going to hard code this right now but in the real world, you would add a form, you would read that form, get the data from that form and then populate the body of this request. Right? So, for now, we are just sending title add post from the front end, content and the status of the post is going to be published. Of course, this can be draft or something else.

And then we just want to return everything and return that response and see how it goes, right?

Now, the only thing we need to do is to connect this function to the button that we created a a little bit earlier. So, I'm just going to add this. So, we are just using query selector to get the button with class of JS add post. And now, we just want to add event listener to that button so that when we click it, it's going to run this function for us.

Okay. Save it and let's check it out if it works.

Okay, I'm going to refresh this. We have this add post button and if I click it, it says we get the response. And this is great because when you get this response, you can use it to maybe show the preview of a post that you're adding or something like that. Whatever you need. So, you get the full response for your post. You get the IDs, everything. Okay. Now, for the real test to see if actually this post is added to our posts. So, if we go right here, we go to posts.

And as you can see right here, it says add post from the front end. If you click on it, we get the content that we added. So, this is the way to add post from your front end, right?

## Working with Custom Post Types

As you can see, this is pretty easy. At least this basic example. You would of course use forms. You would need to handle errors and everything yourself uh when doing this for production, but this is the basic way this works. And uh you can also not just add posts, but you can add other custom post types. For example, we have a post type of products that we used in previous episodes.

Uh so, we have our Where are they? So, products, right? So, these are our products. So, I can add a product right here. Uh and I'm going to use instead of posts right here, I'm just going to say product.

Maybe for you this will be products, books, or something else. Whatever your site needs. So, if I save this again, uh go to my browser, refresh it, and click this, uh we added the post. Now, this post is not inside of posts, but it should be inside of products. As you can see, add posts from the front end. It has the same body, so it's the same post. And that's about it. So, this is the basic way of how you can add uh your content to your WordPress administration using your front end and using WP REST API.

## Conclusion

Okay, so this has been it for this video. Everything we did here will be available for you on GitHub. The link will be in the description below. And as always, thank you guys for watching and I will see you in the next one.
